To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we collected and annotated a new dataset of arguments on Twitter and that we propose an argument mining pipeline that can be applied to this new domain.

(i) the argumentative relations between tweets can be successfully predicted with an F1-score of 0.74, and (ii), the best performing system for this task is a combination of a rule-based approach and a deep learning approach, where the former is used as a feature extractor for the latter.

we created a dataset of arguments mined from tweets and their relations (support and attack) that we used for training and testing argumentation systems and we found that the performance of such systems on Twitter is significantly lower than on traditional texts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1. What are arguments in social media? and 2. Which is the relation between two arguments?

(a) argument identification, which aims at identifying which tweets can be seen as arguments, (b) argument classification, which aims at distinguishing arguments that are supportive or attacking, and (c) argument relation classification, which aims to distinguish between arguments that support or attack each other.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DART is the largest publicly available resource for argument mining on Twitter.
DART is the first resource of natural language tweets annotated for both argument identification and argument relation identification.
DART is a dataset of arguments and their relations on Twitter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we present the first large scale resource for the task of argument mining in social media.
we have created a dataset of 1.5M tweets that contain 1.2M arguments.
DART is a dataset of 2,000 tweets with their corresponding arguments and argument relations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while argumentation is a common practice in Twitter, it is far more common for users to express support for a given claim than for them to argue against it.
, while the problem of identifying arguments on social media is challenging and still open, it is possible to identify the relations between arguments with a reasonable accuracy.

, in contrast to previous work on argument mining, where the arguments are extracted from a corpus of texts, we show that the arguments and their relations can be extracted directly from social media messages.
